name: Internal bleaching
lead: Internal (intracoronal) bleaching is a tooth-whitening procedure for root-canal-treated, non-vital teeth, which lose their nerve supply and often darken [1][2]. The bleaching agent is sealed inside the tooth rather than applied to the outer surface, and is replaced every few weeks until the desired shade is reached; it is most often done on front teeth [2].

Present techniques rely on hydrogen peroxide, applied directly or produced from sodium perborate or carbamide peroxide [3]. A critical review reported more than 90% immediate success for intracoronal bleaching of non-vital teeth, with 10 to 40% of successfully treated teeth needing re-treatment over 1 to 8 years [3].
Cervical root resorption is the best-documented serious risk, linked especially to heated (thermocatalytic) methods [3][4][5].
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide, carbamide peroxide, sodium perborate

paras: In the walking bleach technique, a paste of sodium perborate and water or 3% hydrogen peroxide is placed in the pulp chamber and sealed between visits [5]. Discolouration of non-vital teeth can follow trauma, root canal materials or other causes; case reports describe darkening after white mineral trioxide aggregate and after triple antibiotic paste, and bleaching has been used to treat it [6][7].

The critical review reported over 90% immediate success and re-treatment need in 10 to 40% of cases during 1 to 8 years of follow-up [3]. An analysis of 255 teeth has also been published in the Australian Dental Journal [8].

Cervical root resorption is a possible consequence and is more frequent with thermocatalytic procedures; a 1984 report described external cervical resorption after bleaching a pulpless tooth [3][4][9]. A review of the walking bleach technique advised that heating the mixture is contraindicated because of resorption risk and formation of chemical radicals [5]. Wikipedia also notes intracoronal bleaching may damage dentine and lead to crown brittleness or fracture [2]. Studies have examined the effect of internal bleaching agents on dentinal permeability [10].

A registered trial evaluated intracoronal bleaching of primary anterior teeth after dental trauma in 13 children, with status listed as unknown [11]. The published literature is chiefly reviews, case reports and a retrospective analysis [3][5][8].

timeline.event: A report describes external cervical resorption after bleaching a pulpless tooth.[9]
Reviews of the biological aspects of bleaching and of the walking bleach technique are published.[3][5]

card.summary: Whitening a darkened root-canal-treated tooth from the inside; reported high immediate success, with resorption risk and some re-treatment.
card.aka: Intracoronal bleaching, walking bleach, non-vital bleaching
card.note: Cervical root resorption is a documented risk, especially with heat-activated methods.

quick.overview:
Internal bleaching lightens a dark, root-canal-treated tooth by sealing a peroxide-based agent inside it and changing it over successive visits.

A critical review reported over 90% immediate success, with 10 to 40% of treated teeth needing re-treatment within 1 to 8 years.
quick.mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide, or compounds that release it such as sodium perborate and carbamide peroxide, breaks down the pigment inside the tooth.
quick.risks: Cervical root resorption is the main documented concern, more often with thermocatalytic methods; dentine weakening and crown fracture have also been described.
